title: DOLLAR-COST AVERAGING: DOES IT WORK?

concepts.title: What DCA Means
concepts.body: DCA means investing the same dollars on a schedule — like $833 each month for 12 months to deploy $10,000 — not all at once. You buy fewer shares when prices are high and more when low, smoothing your average cost.

concepts.title: The 68% Rule
concepts.body: Vanguard and Schwab tested rolling 12-month periods from the 1920s onward. Lump sum beat 12-month DCA about two-thirds of the time — about 68% — because markets rise more often than they fall.

concepts.title: $10,000 Head-to-Head
concepts.body: At a steady 7% for illustration, $10,000 invested day one grows to ~$10,700 after 12 months. DCA at end-of-month grows to ~$10,327. The ~$373 gap is not a fee — it is cash drag from money waiting in cash.

concepts.title: See The Cash Drag
concepts.body: Lump sum earns a full year on the whole $10,000. DCA at end-of-month earns about half a year on average — the first $833 earns ~11 months, the last ~0. Later blocks earn less time in the market.

concepts.title: When DCA Helps vs Hurts
concepts.body: DCA helps when you would otherwise stay in cash from fear, or when markets drop right after — less was invested before the fall. It hurts whenever markets rise while cash waits; that ~10% nominal return is the persistent cost.

concepts.title: Use It Right
concepts.body: Automate paycheck investing on payday — no drag. For windfalls, pick a short window (immediate to 6 months) and stick to it. Park waiting cash in yield and check your target, not the entry price.

visual_spec.callout_text: Windfall? Invest promptly or DCA 3–6 months max. Salary? Invest each paycheck — that's drag-free DCA.

sources_footer: Sourced from SEC, FINRA, Vanguard, Charles Schwab, S&P 500 1928–2025
